marble.name: Climate Zones
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Understand that Earth has distinct climate zones — tropical (hot and wet near the equator), temperate (moderate, with four seasons), polar (freezing cold), arid/desert (very dry), and mountain (cold at high altitude) — and that each zone supports different ecosystems and ways of life
marble.prompt: If you looked at a world map showing climate zones, could they explain why the Amazon rainforest, the Sahara desert, and the Arctic all have such different weather, plants, and animals?

cluster.summary: Your child is discovering how weather works — learning about different types of weather, how to stay safe during storms, and understanding how weather patterns change with the seasons.

misconceptions: All deserts are hot — 'desert' means dry; cold/polar deserts exist
Climate zones depend only on latitude — altitude and geography also set them (a tropical mountain can be cold)
Zone boundaries are sharp lines rather than gradual transitions
Temperate = boring/mild everywhere — temperate zones have strong seasons
A zone's plants/animals are there by chance rather than adapted to its climate
representations: World map/globe banded into the climate zones by latitude
Zone cards pairing each zone's climate with its characteristic plants, animals and people
A latitude–altitude grid showing how both together place a zone
Drill-down biome scenes (rainforest, desert, tundra) revealing zone-shaped life
authoredAnswer: No — the equator isn't meaningfully closer to the Sun. Climate zone is decided mainly by latitude: near the equator the Sun's rays hit almost straight down and concentrate heat on a small area, while near the poles the same rays strike at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it's colder. Altitude and distance from the sea also matter.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The equator is the part of Earth nearest the Sun.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: explains climate zones by distance to the Sun
wrongAnswers.fix: Shine a torch straight-on vs slanted onto a globe — slanted light spreads the same heat over more area.

wrongAnswers.wrong: A place's climate zone is whatever the weather is like there today.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: reports today's weather instead of the long-run pattern
wrongAnswers.fix: A zone is the typical climate over many years, not a single day.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: collapses distinct zones such as tropical-wet and arid
wrongAnswers.fix: Contrast a hot-and-wet tropical rainforest with a hot-and-dry desert.
